Crypto speak: Paper hands

You’re already familiar with the term “diamond hands,” but today, we’ll look at its opposite — “paper hands.”

Paper hands are investors who succumb to FOMO and FUD and sell their assets too early because they’re afraid to take risks.

Such depositors start selling off their coins at the first signs of a drop in price.

Remember: Having nerves of steel will serve you better in this industry🙃

🔔 Robert Kiyosaki says cash is trash, backs Bitcoin and Ethereum 

📈 In a June 13 post on X, the Rich Dad Poor Dad author asked how much a trillion dollars is, then used the answer to attack dollar savings.

📊 Kiyosaki wrote that “cash is trash” and said savers of dollars lose purchasing power. He told followers to consider gold, silver, Bitcoin, and Ethereum. His post framed the U.S. dollar as vulnerable because, in his view, the Federal Reserve and U.S. Treasury can create money quickly.

⚠️ His trillion-dollar example also served as a simple visual for readers. By comparing one dollar per minute with the creation of new money, Kiyosaki tried to make a large number feel personal. The post did not include a detailed investment plan. It focused on the idea that cash loses value when supply expands. That framing matches his usual criticism of fiat money. It also fits his asset-focused brand publicly online.

‼️ The warning arrived during a weak period for crypto markets. Bitcoin traded near $64,569 on June 14, while Ethereum traded near $1,674, according to market data. Both assets remained far below their 2025 cycle highs after a sharp June selloff.

Trump’s 60-Day Miracle, Day Zero

The grand Trump–Iran peace sprint can’t even leave the locker room. JD Vance was supposed to land in Zurich, Araghchi was supposed to smile for cameras, the 60-day countdown to “full peace” was supposed to start — instead, both delegations ghosted the Swiss the moment Israel and Hezbollah traded fire in southern Lebanon. The clock is ticking on a deal that hasn’t actually begun.

The whole show is already running on bad faith. Tehran points to the MOU’s first article — “immediate and permanent termination of military operations on all fronts” — and then to fresh Israeli strikes and dead soldiers in Lebanon, and says. 

If Trump can’t control his favorite ally for 48 hours, why should we trust his paperwork for 10 years? Washington, meanwhile, is desperate to reopen Hormuz, cool oil prices and pretend Versailles Sharpie theater equals strategic competence.

Both sides need the deal and don’t believe in it. Iran wants sanctions relief, billions in unfrozen assets and a chance to declare victory after surviving a US–Israeli war that blew up its leadership but not its regime. 

Trump wants to brag that he ended the “biggest energy crisis in history” and defanged Iran’s nuclear program, even as his own advisers admit 60 days is laughable for anything more than a fragile framework glued together by mediators from Pakistan and a Swiss resort concierge.

The real test isn’t uranium or timelines. It’s whether Trump will actually rein in Netanyahu — a country that’s not party to the deal, openly denounces it, and can blow it up any night with a tank, a drone and a press release about “security needs.” 

Iran’s message is brutal and simple: if you can’t leash Israel, you don’t control this agreement; you’re just another signature on a piece of paper we’ve seen you tear up before.

So here we are: 60 days on the brochure, 59 in reality, and already the “historic peace process” looks like every other late‑imperial ritual. A US president signing at Versailles for the cameras, envoys stalled in airports, Swiss hotels waiting with fresh flowers, and a war that still answers to rockets over Lebanon and tankers in Hormuz — not to the pen in Trump’s hand.

🔔 Ripple targets $1B revenue run rate without counting XRP holdings 

❗️ According to posts shared by CoinMarketCap and crypto-focused accounts on X, Ripple expects to end 2026 with a $1 billion revenue run rate. The figure does not include XRP held on Ripple’s balance sheet. That detail matters because Ripple has long faced public debate over the link between its business and XRP. Garlinghouse’s target frames the company as a fintech infrastructure provider that aims to earn money from products, clients, and services, not from token holdings or sales.

🌐 The deal also supports Ripple USD, known as RLUSD. Ripple has promoted the stablecoin for enterprise settlement and collateral use. Recently, crypto news reported that Ripple is also adding RLUSD to new payment tools, including services tied to AI agents and machine payments on the XRP Ledger. Company materials point to custody, treasury management, and liquidity services as core offerings. These products target banks and firms that need faster settlement, account control, and access to digital assets through regulated processes, rather than retail trading.
